non_goals: Grid-level or multi-household forecasting. This is one home, which is far noisier than an aggregate.
Intraday updating. The forecast is issued once, a day ahead.
risks: No weather data. Heating and lighting follow temperature and daylight, which the model can only infer from the calendar.
One household over four years; occupants' routines change and the model assumes the recent past resembles the near future.
Hours with fewer than 45 recorded minutes are dropped, so the longest outages are simply not scored.
lessons: A lag shorter than the forecast horizon is the easiest leak to introduce in time-series work, and here it would have flattered the result substantially.
Averaging the same hour over several weeks is a far stronger baseline than repeating yesterday.
Unlike daily stock returns, household load is genuinely forecastable a day ahead, and learned models beat the baselines by a significant margin.
The best point forecaster was not the best-calibrated one; coverage has to be reported beside loss.
references: Hong, T., & Fan, S. (2016). Probabilistic electric load forecasting: A tutorial review. International Journal of Forecasting, 32(3), 914–938.
